extracted.intended_audience: State Exchanges, Federally Facilitated Exchange (FFE) operators, health insurance issuers, actuarial/policy analysts, and public commenters on the 2026 Payment Notice
extracted.subtask_description: Proposed federal rulemaking (2026 Payment Notice) specifying multiple individual-market Exchange policy changes (OEP timing, SEPs, EHB, premium indexing, AV rules) with associated impact estimates and implementation assumptions, intended for public notice-and-comment.

rubrics_metrics.name: Annual Open Enrollment Period dates (§155.410(e))
rubrics_metrics.description: Change the annual OEP for benefit years starting January 1, 2026 and beyond to begin on November 1 and end on December 15 of the calendar year preceding the benefit year.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Expected to reduce adverse selection, likely lower premiums and PTC costs, increase continuous coverage starting January. Estimated IT implementation: 4,000 hours for the Federal Government and each State Exchange (1,000 hours for a database/network administrator at $101.66/hr and 3,000 hours for a computer programmer at $95.88/hr). For the Federal Government: one-time 4,000 hours costing $389,300. For 20 State Exchanges: aggregate 80,000 hours costing $7,786,000. Total system-update burden estimated at 84,000 hours and $8,175,300. Seek comment on impact estimates, burden, and less burdensome alternatives. Note potential temporary outreach costs to educate consumers; benefits include simplifying operations and eliminating a second January 15 deadline.

rubrics_metrics.name: Repeal 150 percent FPL SEP (§155.420(d)(16))
rubrics_metrics.description: Remove §155.420(d)(16) to repeal the monthly SEP for individuals with projected annual household income at or below 150 percent of the FPL, and make conforming regulatory changes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Rationale: expanded fully-subsidized plan availability plus the 150% FPL SEP opened opportunities for improper enrollments and increased adverse selection. Estimated effects: could decrease premiums by 3–4% vs baseline and reduce annual APTC outlays (approx. $3.4B in 2026, rising thereafter). One-time system cost to remove functionality for Exchanges on the Federal platform estimated at ~$390,000 (assuming 25% database/network admin at $101.66/hr and 75% programmer at $95.88/hr). State Exchanges that implemented the SEP would incur similar costs, though as of Feb 2025 no State Exchanges had offered this SEP. Seek comment on impact estimates and assumptions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Pre-enrollment eligibility verification for SEPs (§155.420)
rubrics_metrics.description: Require all Exchanges to conduct pre-enrollment eligibility verification for SEPs, removing the Federal platform limit to only verify loss of minimum essential coverage SEP; require Exchanges (including State Exchanges) to verify at least 75 percent of new enrollments through SEPs for consumers not already enrolled through that Exchange.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Expected program integrity benefits: reduced improper subsidy payments, modest premium reductions (estimated ~0.5–1.0% for PY2026 and 1.0–2.0% for PY2027+), estimated APTC savings (~$105.4 million). Anticipated burdens: one-time implementation costs (estimated ~$12 million per Exchange for those not previously conducting SEP verification; total $60 million for five State Exchanges), expansion would pend/delay ~293,073 enrollments annually (most delays <1–3 days), estimated annual consumer cost increase from income inconsistencies ~$7,206,665, increased ongoing processing costs for the FFE ~$46.7 million for PY2026–2029, increased annual labor burden on Exchanges using the Federal platform ~$2,833,449 and on State Exchanges ~$1,736,615. One-time development cost for Exchanges on Federal Platform estimated at $1,849,270 (19,000 hours × $97.33). Labor allocation assumptions: 25% database/network admin (hourly $101.66) and 75% computer programmer (hourly $95.88). Seek comment on impact estimates, assumptions, and less burdensome alternatives.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prohibition on sex-trait modification as an EHB (§§156.50 and 156.115(d))
rubrics_metrics.description: Amend §156.115(d) so that an issuer offering EHB may not provide sex-trait modification as an essential health benefit (EHB).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If finalized, sex-trait modification would not be covered as EHB and thus would not receive ACA EHB protections (no annual/lifetime limits, cost-sharing accrual towards annual limitation). Effect on premiums/PTC: plans that stop covering sex-trait modification would see premiums and PTC decrease; plans that cover it as non-EHB would likely see premiums rise or remain the same but PTC would decrease since it would not be EHB. States mandating such coverage beyond EHB would be required to defray costs under §155.170. Utilization is low (approx. 0.11% of enrollees in EDGE data; 0.08–0.09% of allowed costs), so aggregate impact expected to be limited. Seek comment on impact estimates and assumptions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Premium adjustment percentage methodology change (§156.130(e))
rubrics_metrics.description: Propose to use average per-enrollee private health insurance premiums (excluding Medigap and property and casualty insurance) instead of employer-sponsored insurance (ESI) premiums to calculate the premium adjustment percentage for PY2026 and beyond; propose a premium adjustment percentage of 1.6726771319 for PY2026.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consequences: proposed required contribution of 8.05% for PY2026 (vs 7.70% under ESI measure), proposed maximum annual limitation on cost sharing of $10,600 for self-only coverage (vs $10,150 previously). Actuarial/financial impacts estimated: net premium increases of ~ $530 million per year (≈2% of PY2024 net premiums), a decrease in Federal PTC spending between $1.27B and $1.55B annually (2026–2030) assuming Treasury/IRS adopt same measure for section 36B indexing, and estimated Exchange enrollment decline of ~80,000 individuals (PY2026) persisting through 2030. Additional impacts: increased employer shared responsibility payments ($3–$20M/year 2028–2030), potential shifts to short-term plans or uninsured and associated public health/uncompensated care impacts. Seek feedback on impacts and magnitudes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Levels of coverage (Actuarial Value) de minimis range changes (§156.140, §156.200, §156.400)
rubrics_metrics.description: Change de minimis ranges beginning in PY2026 to +2/−4 percentage points for all individual and small group market plans subject to AV requirements (other than expanded bronze), with expanded bronze at +5/−4; remove the +2/0 de minimis range for individual market silver QHPs; define de minimis variation for silver CSR plan variations as +1/−1 percentage points.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Expectation: wider de minimis ranges allow issuers to design lower-AV plans, reducing generosity of out-of-pocket coverage but likely lowering premiums (estimated ~1.0% premium decrease on average). Relationship to subsidies: widening de minimis for silver plans can lower the SLCSP generosity and lead to decreased PTC, generating a short-term transfer from consumers to government/issuers. Changes would not invalidate currently planned health plan designs; issuers can still design plans near the middle of ranges. Effects on ICHRAs: as premiums fall, employer required ICHRA contributions to meet affordability decline, potentially encouraging ICHRA adoption. Seek comment on impact estimates and timing considerations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Regulatory review cost estimation methodology
rubrics_metrics.description: Method for estimating the cost to private entities of reading/interpreting the proposed rule (regulatory review cost).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assumptions: number of reviewers between 266 (unique commenters) and 13,800 (page views) so use average ≈7,000 reviewers; each reviewer reads ~55% of the rule (average of range 10–100%); use BLS wage for medical and health service managers (Code 11-9111) of $106.42/hr (including overhead/fringe); reading speed 250 words/min yields ~3.4 hours to read 55% of the rule; cost per reviewer ≈$361.83 (3.4 × $106.42); total regulatory review cost ≈ $2,532,810. Seek comment on the approach and assumptions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Methodology for quantifying improper enrollments and take-up (use of OEP PUF and ACS/IPUMS)
rubrics_metrics.description: Analytic approach for estimating erroneous and improper enrollments and take-up rates by combining CMS Marketplace Open Enrollment Period (OEP) Public Use Files with IPUMS USA American Community Survey (ACS) samples, adapted from a 2024 AJHE study and a Paragon Health Institute paper.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Key steps/assumptions: use OEP PUFs for plan selections and IPUMS ACS to estimate potentially eligible non-elderly adult populations (exclude Medicare/Medicaid); AJHE additionally excludes employer or TRICARE coverage. For 2024, estimate eligible populations by applying State-level population changes from 2023 to 2024 due to unavailability of 2024 ACS microdata. Exclusions and limitations noted: ACS uses Census poverty definition (differs from MAGI), timing mismatch (ACS asks about previous 12 months), income underreporting in surveys, eligible population may include individuals not eligible for subsidized coverage (affordable employer coverage, unreported Medicaid, immigrants not lawfully present, VA enrollees), and may exclude certain eligible individuals (e.g., some 65+). Specific states excluded where appropriate (Minnesota, New York, Oregon due to BHP; DC due to insufficient income info; Idaho 2019 missing). Analysts acknowledge these limitations and seek comment on improving analyses (e.g., multi-year ACS or refined income/family unit measures).

rubrics_metrics.name: Implementation cost and labor-allocation assumptions for IT and system changes
rubrics_metrics.description: Standard assumptions used across multiple proposals to estimate one-time and ongoing IT/system development costs and staff burden.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Common assumptions: allocate 25% of hours to a database/network administrator (hourly wage $101.66) and 75% to a computer programmer (hourly wage $95.88), based on past system changes. Examples applying this assumption: OEP system change (4,000 hours) cost to Federal Gov't $389,300; 20 State Exchanges aggregate 80,000 hours costing $7,786,000 (total 84,000 hours, $8,175,300). Repeal of 150% FPL SEP estimated one-time cost ~$390,000 using same allocation. Pre-enrollment SEP verification expansion assumed 19,000 hours × $97.33 to estimate one-time development cost for Exchanges using Federal Platform ($1,849,270). Seek comment on these estimates and allocation assumptions.
